facts.claim: "Western Skies" is track 5 on Dustin Kensrue's album Desert Dreaming, released April 5, 2024.

Dustin Kensrue is credited as composer and producer on Desert Dreaming. The credits also list Matthew Barnhart (engineer), Scott Evans (mixing), Abe Levy (pedal steel), James McAlister (drums), Seth Richardson (double bass) and Cat Clyde (featured vocals).
The album is self-produced. Kensrue made it with upright bassist Seth Richardson, pedal steel guitarist Abe Levy and drummer James McAlister.
Kensrue wrote the album on acoustic guitar and recorded most of it at home.

Kensrue said "the setting really is the main character of the record." The ten songs mix biography, history and fiction and were partly inspired by childhood trips to the desert to see his grandparents.
Kensrue described the desert on the record as both a literal place and a metaphor for being present and waking up to what is in front of you.

The Scope Of called "Western Skies" an ominous ballad of reflection and regret that would make Johnny Cash proud. Sputnikmusic said it and "The Heart of Sedona" stand out for their vocal performances.
Kensrue performed "Western Skies" and "The Heart of Sedona" in a video session for The Noise. The session was framed around country legends such as Johnny Cash, Gene Autry and Patsy Cline.
Desert Dreaming is Kensrue's third solo studio album. Press material says it leans heavily on the country and western music of the 1950s and 60s.
Kensrue is best known as the frontman of the post-hardcore band Thrice. He grew up in Southern California as a punk-rock-raised teenager who avoided country music.

draft:
The joke in the chorus lands like a punch. **"Western Skies"** spends two verses on a familiar cowboy fantasy, freedom and open country and riding until the mountains rise, then lets its narrator name the culprits for how it all went wrong: "Double-crossed by my blood / And some goddamn country song." It's self-pity with a sense of humor, and also a confession. He blames his restless nature, he blames the myth of the lone rider he soaked up from records, and underneath both he knows he chose this.

The cruelest detail is in the first verse. The love at home didn't fight the leaving. They said they'd "never been a fan of fences" and told him to go see what he could see. That generosity is what wrecks him later, when he realizes he never had to choose between the horizon and the person who already let him roam. By the fifth verse he's tossing down empty bottles at Angel's Landing, admitting the view must be lovely but he can't see it through his tears. Kensrue has said the desert on this record is both a real place and a metaphor for waking up to what's in front of you. This narrator wakes up too late, staring at a vista he can't take in.

The last verse is where the language goes old-fashioned and biblical: "The band on my Stetson like thorns on my brow." The cowboy hat turns into a crown of thorns, and the costume of freedom becomes a penance. In the final chorus the line shrinks, losing the curse and the "country," as if he's run out of the energy to blame the genre and only the bare fact of the song is left.

The sound stays out of his way. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through bright arpeggios, a bass holds down the low end, and the tempo is slow and unhurried. Nothing builds or drops out. The room feels close and natural, which fits a record Kensrue wrote on acoustic guitar and mostly cut at home. His voice is clear with a slight rasp, sung alone with no harmonies, deliberate and almost crooning. Sputnikmusic picked this as one of the album's standout vocal turns, and The Scope Of heard a ballad that would make Johnny Cash proud.

That Cash comparison is earned. Kensrue, the Thrice frontman who grew up a punk kid steering clear of country, built *Desert Dreaming* on the country and western of the 1950s and '60s. He doesn't wink at the form. He takes its lonesome-rider archetype and asks what it costs the people left at home.

The song gets under your skin by letting a man laugh bitterly at the songs that made leaving look noble, right up until he can't see the view he gave everything up for.
